extracted.intended_audience: general readers and writers interested in Australian Aboriginal culture, Dreaming, and songlines
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for depicting or understanding Aboriginal songlines: their nature as paths of Creator-beings, how songs encode landscape and culture, and the social, ceremonial and navigational roles they play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a songline
rubrics_metrics.description: A songline, also called dreaming track, is one of the paths across the land (or sometimes the sky) within the animist belief systems of the Aboriginal cultures of Australia which mark the route followed by localised 'creator-beings' in the Dreaming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Songlines are recorded in traditional song cycles, stories, dance, and art, and are often the basis of ceremonies. When representing songlines, treat them as culturally embedded routes tied to creation narratives and ritual practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Songlines link places and Creation events
rubrics_metrics.description: Songlines connect places and Creation events, and the ceremonies associated with those places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray songlines as tying specific landscape features to ancestral actions; ceremonies are enacted at particular places along songlines and are part of maintaining those connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Songs encode navigational information
rubrics_metrics.description: A knowledgeable person is able to navigate across the land by repeating the words of the song, which describe the location of landmarks, waterholes, and other natural phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By singing the songs in the appropriate sequence, Aboriginal people could navigate vast distances. Represent songs as practical mnemonic maps that specify landmarks and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melodic contour and rhythm overcomes language differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Since a songline can span the lands of several different language groups, different parts of the song are said to be in those different languages... Languages are not a barrier because the melodic contour of the song describes the nature of the land over which the song passes. The rhythm is what is crucial to understanding the song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing cross-linguistic songlines, emphasize melody/rhythm and musical shape as carriers of meaning rather than literal lexical translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Songlines as social protocol / cultural passport
rubrics_metrics.description: Songlines have been described as a 'cultural passport' which, when sung in the language of a particular region and mob, show respect to the people of that country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict singing appropriate parts of songlines as a form of social recognition and respect between neighbouring groups; songs encode obligations and reciprocal relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directionality and sacredness
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases, a songline has a particular direction, and walking the wrong way along a songline may be a sacrilegious act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent direction and correct sequence as important: singing and traveling in proper order can have moral or sacred consequences. Songs are continually sung to keep the land 'alive'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to country and identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Their 'connection to country' describes a strong and complex relationship with the land of their ancestors, or 'mob'. Aboriginal identity often links to their language groups and traditional country of their ancestors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray songlines as central to identity and belonging; they express connectedness to country and are transmitted within families and groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Songlines as repositories of knowledge and survival information
rubrics_metrics.description: Songlines can be visualised as corridors or pathways of knowledge that crisscross the entire continent, sky and water... These sites of significance, formed by ancestral beings, are like libraries, storing critical knowledge for survival. The stories at significant sites contain knowledge that instruct on social behaviour, gender relations or where water or food can be sourced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize the practical, instructional role of songlines: they encode ecological, social and gendered knowledge essential for living in particular landscapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic and mythical referents in songs
rubrics_metrics.description: Most songs... have a geographical as well as mythical referent, so by learning the songline men become familiar with literally thousands of sites even though they have never visited them; all become part of their cognitive map of the desert world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict songs as containing both mythic narratives and precise geographic markers that produce a cognitive map for listeners and singers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical marks and landscape features as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases, the paths of the creator-beings are said to be evident from their marks, or petrosomatoglyphs, on the land, such as large depressions in the land which are said to be their footprints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing songlines, include physical markers (rock impressions, engravings, depressions) that anchor ancestral narratives to tangible landscape features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation by landscape and local practice
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Sydney region... songlines tend to follow the ridge lines... In contrast, in many other parts of Australia, the songlines tend to follow valleys, where water may be found more easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for regional differences: geological and ecological conditions shape the routes and associated art; avoid a one-size-fits-all depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Songlines enable intergroup travel and exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: The continent of Australia contains an extensive system of songlines... some traverse hundreds of kilometres through lands of many different Aboriginal peoples — peoples who may speak markedly different languages and have different cultural traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent long-distance songlines as networks that enabled trade, knowledge exchange, and shared ceremonial obligations across language groups and environments.
